flashcards.q: List the XSS sinks that matter in a modern frontend codebase.
flashcards.a: innerHTML/outerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, eval/new Function, document.write, javascript: URLs in href/src, and string-argument setTimeout/setInterval.

flashcards.q: Why does React's default JSX rendering avoid the most common XSS class?
flashcards.a: JSX text interpolation ({value} as a child) auto-escapes by default -- the vulnerability requires someone to deliberately opt into dangerouslySetInnerHTML, a different security posture than hand-written template strings.

flashcards.q: Why is strict-dynamic + nonce preferred over a host-allowlist CSP?
flashcards.a: Host allowlists break constantly because third-party scripts load further scripts from unanticipated origins, and any allowlisted domain with an open redirect or upload path becomes a bypass. strict-dynamic propagates trust cryptographically from a nonce'd root script instead.

flashcards.q: What must be true of a CSP nonce for it to actually work?
flashcards.a: It must be cryptographically random and freshly generated PER HTTP RESPONSE. A static or reused nonce defeats the mechanism entirely.

flashcards.q: What does CORS actually protect against, and what's the common misconception?
flashcards.a: CORS is a browser-side restriction on whether client-side JS can READ a cross-origin response. It does NOT stop the request from being sent or processed server-side -- the request still reaches the server and any side effect (e.g. a DB write) still happens; the browser only blocks the calling script from reading the response.

flashcards.q: Why is dynamically reflecting the request's Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin dangerous even though it's not the literal wildcard *?
flashcards.a: It reintroduces the same vulnerability the spec's block on '* + credentials:true' is meant to prevent -- any origin can make a credentialed cross-origin request and read the response -- while looking superficially compliant since it's not technically '*'.

flashcards.q: What is the 2026 practitioner consensus for auth token storage?
flashcards.a: Short-lived access token in JS memory only (gone on reload, minimizes exfiltration window) plus a longer-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite cookie (invisible to JS), with CSRF protection on state-changing endpoints since the cookie is auto-attached by the browser.

flashcards.q: Why is storing an auth token in localStorage widely considered a mistake?
flashcards.a: localStorage is readable by any successful XSS -- an XSS bug anywhere on the page becomes a full, silent account takeover, since there's no HttpOnly equivalent for localStorage.

flashcards.q: What is clickjacking mechanically, and what's the current correct defense header?
flashcards.a: An attacker embeds the target site in an invisible/positioned iframe, overlays decoy UI, and tricks a user into clicking a hidden real button. Defense: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' (wins over legacy X-Frame-Options in all CSP2+ browsers).

flashcards.q: Why does setting X-Frame-Options via a <meta> tag not work?
flashcards.a: X-Frame-Options is only honored as a real HTTP response header; a <meta http-equiv> tag has no effect on it -- a common real-world implementation mistake.

flashcards.q: Describe the September 2025 npm supply-chain incident and what it demonstrates.
flashcards.a: A phishing attack against one npm maintainer compromised 18 packages (chalk, debug, ansi-styles, strip-ansi -- 2.6B combined weekly downloads) with a crypto-wallet-targeting payload, followed by the self-propagating Shai-Hulud worm (500+ packages wave 1, tens of thousands of repos by "2.0" in Nov 2025). It demonstrates risk lives in TRANSITIVE dependencies teams never directly import.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't SameSite=Lax alone fully solve CSRF?
flashcards.a: SameSite=Lax still allows top-level GET navigations to carry the cookie (e.g. a malicious link top-level-navigating to a state-changing GET endpoint), and browser enforcement nuances exist -- an explicit CSRF token (synchronizer or double-submit cookie pattern) on state-changing endpoints is needed for a complete answer.

flashcards.q: Why is checking event.source instead of event.origin insufficient in a postMessage handler?
flashcards.a: event.source identifies which window object sent the message but says nothing about that window's origin (which can also change via navigation after the reference was captured) -- origin validation and source validation solve different problems; skipping the origin check leaves message forgery from any origin possible.

flashcards.q: What does Subresource Integrity (SRI) protect against for a third-party CDN-hosted script tag?
flashcards.a: A compromised CDN or vendor account silently swapping the script content. The browser computes a hash of the fetched script and refuses to execute it if it doesn't match the integrity attribute's hash, failing closed instead of silently executing tampered code.
